newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil farmers mull impact of new import rules.
newsitem.headline: Brazil farmers mull impact of new import rules.

text.p: Brazilian farmers may have to start growing more cotton and wheat since a government move to clamp down on short-term financing for imports will likely make commodity imports more expensive, analysts said.
For goods shipped from April 1, the central bank will require importers with less than 360-day financing to pay for their foreign currency the day they pick up their merchandise from customs.
Industry sources said it was too early to gauge the possible impact on imports of commodities but said cotton and wheat were likely to be more affected than soybeans or corn, for instance.

"This represents an advantage for domestic wheat producers, who have been pressuring the government for measures to stimulate national production," said Gil Barabach, analyst at independent consultants Safras e Mercado.
The average financing period for wheat imports was 180 days at an interest rate of eight percent, meaning they fall under the umbrella of the new legislation.

But it was too late to change planting intentions for the current harvest so that low domestic stocks will keep Brazil reliant on Argentine imports for a large proportion of its domestic consumption, Barabach said.
"For this harvest, it has no choice. But what could happen is that in the next harvest, (the new law) will incentivise domestic production," he added.

Cotton importers could also find it more difficult to trade under the new law, although with an average financing period of 360 days, large firms will be able to negotiate a 20 to 30 day extension which will allow them to narrowly escape the rules.

Brazil is expected to be the world's largest importer of cotton in 1997 as its harvest plummets to its lowest level in 20 years, with Paraguay and Argentina providing the bulk of a forecast 500,000 tonnes of imports, industry sources said.

"The big importers will remain free of this legislation, and those who will suffer from it are the small and medium-sized importers," said Hugo Sergio Nieri of brokerage Nieri Corretora, adding that large importers represent more than half the market.
An added side-effect could be a rise in internal cotton prices, said Paulo Molinari, analyst at Safras e Mercado.

"It will have an impact at the level of imports but also on internal cotton prices," said Molinari, pointing out that while the government was bringing its ballooning trade deficit under control, it was letting inflation rise.
Corn imports were seen mostly unaffected by the measure.
"Since last year, you can only import corn with immediate payment but the market has ways of escaping these conditions by using credit cards," Molinari said.

"In Brazil, in the case of corn the government is conducting an internal subsidy policy aimed at the north and north-east, which is the main importer of Argentine corn, to discourage them from importing from Argentina," he said.
That policy was having more impact than any generalised law on imports would, he added.
Soybean imports could also be hit, although it was too early to say to which extent, said Cesar Borges de Souza, president of the Brazilian Association of Vegetable Oils Industries (Abiove).
"This tends to reduce imports but by how much will depend largely on how companies are going to react," de Souza said.
"In this harvest there is a great pressure to sell and a natural movement of the product out of the country. So we will always have these imports (in between harvests)," he said.
